teaser: In 2022 a museum cut this painting into 10,000 digital pieces. People bought them as love tokens.
review_notes:
Claim that 25,000 crowns was far above any earlier price for a painting in Vienna: commonly repeated, confirm.
Belvedere NFT drop: 14 February 2022, 10,000 tiles, 1,850 euros each. Confirm figures.
Purchase by the Austrian state at the 1908 Kunstschau for 25,000 crowns, before the painting was finished.
Materials: oil with gold, silver and platinum leaf on canvas, 180 x 180 cm.
Klimt's two trips to Ravenna dated 1903.
The plants are described loosely (vine or ivy leaves in his hair); botanical identification is not certain.

lesson.text: On Valentine's Day 2022, the Belvedere museum in Vienna sliced a digital copy of this painting into a grid of 10,000 tiles and sold each one as an NFT, a certificate of digital ownership, for 1,850 euros. You could dedicate your square to someone you love. Few paintings could carry that idea. This one has been on mugs, umbrellas and dorm-room walls for a century.

The real object is harder to own. It is a square canvas 180 centimeters on each side (almost 6 ft), and it is covered not only in oil paint but in thin sheets of real gold, with touches of silver and platinum. Gustav Klimt finished it in 1908, at the height of what is called his golden period.
Gold was a family matter. Klimt's father, Ernst, was a gold engraver, and Gustav trained at Vienna's school of applied arts, a school for craftsmen and decorators, not at the fine art academy.
Start with the two bodies, which is harder than it sounds: where does he end and where does she begin? Klimt wraps them in a single golden shape, then tells them apart with pattern alone.

lesson.title: Two robes
lesson.text: One cloak of gold, two different languages of ornament.

spots.title: His side
spots.text: Hard-edged rectangles in black, white and silver, stacked upright. Klimt gives the man straight lines and sharp corners.

spots.title: Her side
spots.text: Circles and clusters of flowers in red, violet and blue. Her dress is all curves, and it clings to the body where his robe hides it.

spots.title: The seam
spots.text: Where the two meet, their hands touch and the patterns begin to mix: small squares drift onto her shoulder, gold spirals creep across his robe.

lesson.text: The patterns are a code that viewers in 1908 would have read at once: rigid for him, flowing for her. You may find that division dated today. But notice that the faces tell a less tidy story than the clothes do.

You never see the man's face. He turns it away, and all Klimt shows is a strong neck and a crown of leaves. The woman's face is the only one offered to you, eyes closed, tilted flat against the picture like an icon.
How do two people become one form?

lines.label: One column
lines.text: The golden cloak closes around both figures like a bell. From a distance you read a single upright shape before you read two people.

lines.label: Two heads
lines.text: His head bends down and over, hers falls back at a right angle. The line through them is broken, almost a corner. It is not an entirely comfortable pose.

lines.label: The ledge
lines.text: The flowered meadow stops at the right, as if it were the edge of a cliff. Beyond it there is only gold.

lesson.text: That ledge changes the mood. The lovers are not in a garden; they are at the brink of something, kneeling on the last patch of ground. And one part of her body shows she knows it.
Most of her body is hidden under the dress. Find her bare feet.

spots.title: Toes at the edge
spots.text: Her feet hang past the end of the meadow, and her toes curl hard, gripping. Thin gold chains of leaves trail down from her ankles. She is kneeling. If she stood up, she would be taller than him.

lesson.text: Curled toes, a clenched hand on his neck, a face turned to the side: is she melting into the embrace or bracing against it? Klimt left both readings open, and people have argued about it ever since. The painting is more than a greeting card because of this doubt.

The Austrian state bought the painting straight off the wall of the 1908 Vienna Kunstschau, the exhibition where it was first shown, before Klimt had even finished it. The price was 25,000 crowns, far more than had ever been paid for a painting in Vienna.

The purchase was a kind of peace offering. A few years earlier, Klimt's ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna had been attacked as ugly and obscene, and in 1905 he angrily gave the commission back. With this canvas, the official scandal became a national treasure.

Where did the idea of a painting made of gold come from? In 1903 Klimt traveled twice to Ravenna in Italy and stood under church mosaics made in the 500s, where saints and empresses float on walls of gold glass. He brought home the flat, shining, timeless space of those walls, and put lovers in it instead of saints.
Gold erases place and time. With no room, no sky and no shadow, the couple is nowhere in particular, which is why anyone can step into their place.

The surface is not one gold but many. Some areas are smooth leaf, some are raised, and the background is dusted with flecks like a night sky. Wander across it and see how much variety Klimt gets from a single metal.

spots.title: Crown of leaves
spots.text: Green leaves are woven through his dark curls, like the wreath of an ancient god of wine and revelry. It is all the portrait you get of him.

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Closed eyes, flushed cheek, small flowers scattered in red hair. Skin is painted softly and realistically; everything around it is flat ornament.

spots.title: Her hand
spots.text: Her fingers hook around the back of his neck, bent at the knuckles. A tense little hand in a picture famous for tenderness.

spots.title: Gold dust
spots.text: The background is a darker, bronze-toned gold sprinkled with bright flecks. It reads as air, or as night, or as nothing at all.

spots.title: The meadow
spots.text: A carpet of violet, blue and yellow blossoms, painted in dabs of oil. It is the one area that looks like the natural world.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: GUSTAV KLIMT, stacked in two lines of block letters and set in a corner of the gold like a goldsmith's stamp.

lesson.text: Klimt painted in a long, loose blue smock that reached his ankles, working in a garden studio in Vienna and sharing the place with a number of cats.

quiz.question: How does Klimt tell the man's robe from the woman's dress?
options: By color: his is silver, hers is gold
By pattern: rectangles for him, circles and flowers for her
By outline: a black line separates them
quiz.explanation: Both are gold; only the ornament differs.

quiz.question: What inspired the flat golden space of the painting?
options: Japanese folding screens seen in Paris
quiz.explanation: Klimt visited Ravenna twice in 1903 and saw its gold mosaics.

quiz.question: What do the woman's feet do?
options: Curl over the edge of the meadow
quiz.explanation: Her toes grip the last bit of ground where the meadow stops.

quiz.question: Who bought the painting in 1908?
quiz.explanation: The state bought it at the Kunstschau before it was finished.

quiz.question: Whose face is fully visible?
quiz.explanation: The man turns away; only his neck and wreath show.

facts.text: The gold in The Kiss is yellow oil paint mixed to look metallic.
facts.explanation: Klimt applied sheets of real gold leaf, with some silver and platinum.

facts.text: The woman in the painting is kneeling.
facts.explanation: Her feet trail behind her at the meadow's edge; standing, she would be taller than the man.

facts.text: Klimt studied at Vienna's academy of fine arts.
facts.explanation: He trained at the school of applied arts, a school for craftsmen and decorators.
